parameters.content:
## Log cleaning enquiries to Google Sheets and auto-reply with Gmail

**Who's it for**
Commercial cleaning companies, and any small service business, whose website form fills up faster than anyone can answer it.

**How it works**
Your website form posts to the webhook. `read the form fields` reads the payload whatever the plugin calls its fields - Contact Form 7, WPForms, Gravity Forms, Elementor and Fluent Forms all land cleanly - then honeypot hits and anything with no usable email are dropped. The postcode picks the area owner. The row is written to Google Sheets **before any email is attempted**, so an enquiry can never be lost to a mail failure. The customer gets a plain acknowledgement asking the three questions you always end up asking anyway; the owner gets the details and the reference.

**How to set up**
1. Create a sheet with an `Enquiries` tab and the column headings listed in `config`.
2. Attach a Google Sheets credential and a Gmail credential to the three `[cred]` nodes.
3. Open `config` and set `TRACKER_SHEET_ID`, the `AREAS` postcode table and your company details.
4. Point your form plugin at this workflow's webhook URL.

**Requirements**
A Google Sheets credential, a Gmail credential, and a website form that can POST the submission as JSON.

**How to customize**
`QUESTIONS` and `AREAS` in `config` change what you ask and who quotes where. The email wording lives in `write the first reply`.

## Nothing is sent until you say so

`TEST_RUN = true` with a blank `TEST_EMAIL` - how it ships - writes the sheet row but sends no email. Open **STOP: preview - nothing sent** to read exactly what the customer and the owner would have got.

Put your own address in `TEST_EMAIL` and the emails really send, but every one goes to you instead of the customer. `TEST_RUN = false` goes live.

### 1. Take the enquiry in and check it is real

`Enquiry arrives` is the webhook your website form posts to. `config` holds every setting in one place: the sheet id, the postcode table, your company details and the safety switch.

`read the form fields` does not care which form plugin you use. It looks for each field by the names plugins commonly give it, then falls back to the shape of the value, so numbered fields still work. `a real enquiry?` drops honeypot hits and anything with no usable email address at **STOP: spam or incomplete**.

### 2. Pick the owner, write the reply, log the row

`assign an owner` matches the postcode against the `AREAS` table, longest prefix first, so a rule for `SW1` beats a rule for `SW`. Nothing falls through; an unmatched postcode goes to the fallback owner.

`write the first reply` builds both emails: the customer acknowledgement with your three questions, and the internal heads-up. `row for the sheet` shapes one row and `[cred] Sheets - log the enquiry` appends it **before any email is attempted**, so a mail failure can never lose an enquiry.

### 3. Send the two emails, or hold them back

`sending?` reads the safety switch in `config`. In preview mode everything stops at **STOP: preview - nothing sent**, with both drafts on the item so you can read exactly what would have gone out.

`[cred] Gmail - reply to the customer` sends the acknowledgement. `owner has an email?` then checks the area owner actually has an address; if not the branch ends quietly at **STOP: no owner email set** instead of failing the run. `[cred] Gmail - tell the owner` sends the internal note.

### 4. Answer the website form

`Reply to the website` returns a small JSON body with the reference back to the form plugin.

Every path reaches it - accepted, spam, preview and no-owner alike - so the visitor always sees a success message and never a timeout.

The reference is the same short code written to the sheet, so a customer can read it out on the phone.
